etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English daschen, dassen, from Danish daske (“to slap, strike”), related to Swedish daska (“to smack, slap, spank”), of obscure origin. Compare German tatschen (“to grope, paw”), Old English dwǣsċan (“to quell, put out, destroy, extinguish”). See also dush.

definitions.definition: (typography) Any of the following symbols: ‒ (figure dash), – (en dash), — (em dash), or ― (horizontal bar).
(by extension) The longer of the two symbols of Morse code.

definitions.definition: A small quantity of a liquid substance etc.; less than 1/8 of a teaspoon.
(Nigeria, Ghana, Liberia) A bribe or gratuity; a gift.

quote.citation: 1992, George Billy Nii Ayittey, Africa Betrayed, →ISBN, →OCLC, →OL, page 44:
quote.text: The traditional practice of offering gifts or "dash" to chiefs has often been misinterpreted by scholars to provide a cultural explanation for the pervasive incidence of bribery and corruption in modern Africa.

quote.citation: 2006, Adiele Eberechukwu Afigbo, The Abolition of the Slave Trade in Southeastern Nigeria, 1885–1950 (Rochester Studies in African History and the Diaspora; 25), University of Rochester Press, →ISBN, →ISSN, page 99:
quote.text: Writing in 1924 on a similar situation in Ugep, the political officer, Mr. S. T. Harvey noted: "In the old days there was no specified dowry but merely dashes given to the father-in-law, from 8 to 20 rods according to the status of the man […] The dowry is made small because whatsoever a woman farms or reaps during her life time is by native custom the property of her parents."

quote.citation: 2008, Lizzie Williams, updated by Mark Shenley, Nigeria: The Bradt Travel Guide, published 2012, →ISBN, →OCLC, →OL, page 109:
quote.text: The only other times you'll be asked for a dash is from beggars.

definitions.definition: (dated, euphemistic) A stand-in for a censored word, like "Devil" or "damn". (Compare deuce.)

quote.citation: 1853, William Makepeace Thackeray, The Newcomes, Chapter VI, serialized in Harper's New Monthly Magazine, (VIII, no. 43, Dec 1853) p. 118
quote.text:
Sir Thomas looks as if to ask what the dash is that to you! but wanting still to go to India again, and knowing how strong the Newcomes are in Leadenhall Street, he thinks it necessary to be civil to the young cub, and swallows his pride once more into his waistband.
Comment: Some editions leave this passage out. Of those that include it, some change the 'you!' to 'you?'.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To run quickly or for a short distance.

quote.citation: 1961 November, H. G. Ellison, P. G. Barlow, “Journey through France: Part One”, in Trains Illustrated, page 670:
quote.text: As our train to Paris dashed through the labyrynthine flyovers at Porchefontaine, barely a mile from Versailles, the 75 m.p.h. limit was already almost attained.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive, sometimes figurative) To sprinkle; to splatter.

definitions.definition: (transitive, dated) To mix, reduce, or adulterate, by throwing in something of an inferior quality.
(transitive, of hopes or dreams) To ruin; to destroy.

definitions.definition: (transitive, usually with down or off) To complete hastily.
(transitive) To draw or write quickly; jot.
